summary: Defines Management Information Base objects for managing Session Initiation Protocol entities, including user agents, proxy servers, redirect servers and registrars, with network management protocols such as SNMP.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP sets up internet phone calls. This note lists the gauges and settings a manager can read on call servers and phones, so they can check how things are running.

questions: how to monitor sip servers with snmp
what mib modules does rfc 4780 define
subtitle: SNMP objects for monitoring and configuring SIP user agents, proxies, redirect servers and registrars.

tldr.problem: Operators of SIP user agents and servers had no standard way to read their status and statistics or to configure them with network management tools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four SMIv2 MIB modules (SIP-TC-MIB, SIP-COMMON-MIB, SIP-UA-MIB and SIP-SERVER-MIB) with configuration objects, statistics tables and notifications, and ties each SIP entity to the NETWORK-SERVICES-MIB.
tldr.outcome: A device can expose several SIP entities through one SNMP agent, but the objects need protection, and the RFC recommends SNMPv3 with cryptographic security.

today: RFC 4780 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of these SIP MIB modules as far as this text and metadata say.

sections.title: Scope of the SIP MIB
sections.content:
This memo defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols. It describes managed objects for Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) entities: User Agents, and Proxy, Redirect and Registrar servers. SIP itself, defined in RFC 3261, is an application-layer signaling protocol for creating, modifying and terminating sessions such as Internet telephone calls, multimedia distribution and multimedia conferences.

The objects give basic SIP protocol management: monitoring of status and protocol statistics, and configuration of SIP entities. Management of application-specific or service-specific SIP configuration is out of scope.

The modules follow SMIv2 (STD 58, made up of RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580), and the objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).
sections.plainLanguage: SIP phones and call servers are like machines with dials on them. This document says what the dials are called so every manager can read them the same way.

sections.title: The Four MIB Modules
sections.content:
Four modules are specified. SIP-TC-MIB defines the textual conventions used by the others. SIP-COMMON-MIB holds objects common to all SIP entities. SIP-UA-MIB is specific to User Agents, and SIP-SERVER-MIB is specific to Proxy, Redirect and Registrar servers.

To conform, an SNMP agent MUST implement SIP-TC-MIB, SIP-COMMON-MIB and one of the entity-type-specific modules (SIP-SERVER-MIB or SIP-UA-MIB) for each instance of a SIP entity being managed. A device with more than one SIP entity MUST implement multiple SIP modules.

The common module is split into object groups for base configuration (protocol version, entity type, operational and administrative status, organization name, maximum transactions), timer configuration, summary statistics, per-method statistics, status code statistics, current transactions, retransmissions and other statistics, plus objects that are accessible only through notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four binders of rules. One explains the words, one covers things every SIP device has, one covers phones, and one covers servers. A device uses the binders that fit it.

sections.title: Several Entities in One Device
sections.content:
A design requirement was that a single system with a single SNMP agent can support multiple instances of the SIP MIB modules. That is done with the Network Services Monitoring MIB (NETWORK-SERVICES-MIB, RFC 2788). A device implementing the SIP MIB MUST support it and, at a minimum, the applIndex and applName objects of its application table (applTable). Each SIP entity then gets its own row, and the same applIndex is used in the SIP tables.

A naming convention SHOULD make each applName unique. A proxy name starts with sip_proxy, a registrar with sip_registrar, a user agent with sip_ua, each followed by an instance identifier, such as sip_proxy1 or sip_ua2. For a combined server, the RECOMMENDED order is proxy first, redirect second and registrar last, as in sip_proxy_redirect_registrar2.

If supported, applUptime MUST equal sipCommonCfgServiceStartTime, and applLastChange MUST equal sipCommonCfgServiceLastChange. applOperStatus SHOULD reflect sipCommonCfgServiceOperStatus through a mapping. The RFC gives two examples: a proxy and a registrar kept as separate SIP-COMMON-MIB instances, and one shared instance (sip_proxy_registrar1).
sections.plainLanguage: If one computer runs a few SIP helpers, each helper gets its own name tag, like sip_ua1 and sip_ua2, so a manager can tell their dials apart.

sections.title: What the Modules Expose
sections.content:
Beyond the base configuration, SIP-COMMON-MIB lists the ports an entity listens on, the option tags it supports, and the SIP methods it supports. The supported-methods table is informational: it is populated by the system, and an SNMP manager cannot add or delete entries. It reports the operational status of the service as unknown, up, down, congested, restarting, quiescing or testing.

The statistics cover total requests and responses in and out, total transactions, inbound and outbound counts per method, retransmissions, counts of responses by status code, a gauge of transactions awaiting definitive responses, and counts of requests with unsupported URIs or unsupported methods.

SIP-UA-MIB has a table of servers a user agent uses, each with an address type, an address and a role. SIP-SERVER-MIB covers the server host address, proxy settings such as authentication methods and realm, and registrar settings.

A proxy reports a default mode that is stateless, transactionStateful or callStateful. A registrar reports the maximum contact expiry a user agent may request, the maximum number of users it supports and the current number of users, and a per-user table of registrations.
sections.plainLanguage: The dials show if the server is up, how many calls it has handled, what kinds of messages it knows, and who is signed in.

sections.title: Handling New SIP Methods
sections.content:
SIP methods can be added by other RFCs, and more may be defined in the future. To avoid updating SIP-COMMON-MIB for each one, methods are named with the SipTCMethodName textual convention, which represents any method registered with IANA. It is an octet string of 1 to 100 characters.

The convention allows experimental extension methods. An object using it MAY return or accept a value not sanctioned by IANA, and the system MUST ensure no collisions with officially assigned method names. In the supported-methods table, values such as ACK, BYE, CANCEL, INVITE and OPTIONS can appear.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of printing a fixed list of moves, the form has a blank for the move name, so new moves can be written in later.

sections.title: Notifications for Status Codes
sections.content:
SIP-COMMON-MIB defines notifications. sipCommonStatusCodeNotif signals that a specific status code has been sent or received. Two threshold notifications, one for inbound and one for outbound responses, signal that a status code was seen often enough to exceed the configured threshold, and can serve as an early warning in place of the first. Further notifications cover service cold start, warm start and status change.

Which status codes are monitored is configured by the manager. For emission, the sipCommonStatusCodeNotifEmitMode object is normal (a notification for each matching response), oneShot (only the next matching response, which limits promiscuous behavior) or triggered (read-only, showing that a one-shot has fired and the mode must be reset). Setting sipCommonStatusCodeNotifSend to true is required for these modes to have any effect.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask the server to ring a bell when a certain message shows up too many times, or just once, so it does not ring all day.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Several read-write and read-create objects can be sensitive. If sipCommonStatusCodeRowStatus is set maliciously, the system may over-allocate resources to keep statistics. If the notification-control objects (such as sipCommonStatusCodeNotifSend and sipCommonCfgServiceNotifEnable) are set maliciously, SNMP notifications can hurt system and network performance.

Readable objects can also leak information. Some may hold private data, such as sipServerRegContactURI and sipCommonCfgOrganization. Status, entity type and supported methods may help attackers plan attacks: a congested status invites overload attacks, and a method list can help build method-specific attacks.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS that implementers consider SNMPv3 security features, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms, and says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must make sure only principals with legitimate rights can GET or SET the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The dials and switches should be locked in a cabinet. Otherwise a stranger could read private things or flip switches to cause trouble.

sections.title: IANA Object Identifiers
sections.content: The modules use object identifier values recorded in the SMI Numbers registry, all under mib-2: sipTC is 148, sipCommonMIB is 149, sipUAMIB is 150 and sipServerMIB is 151.
sections.plainLanguage: Each of the four binders got its own number in the big registry so nobody else uses it.
